events.title: The battle of Chrysopolis
events.shortBlurb: Constantine's final victory over Licinius on the Bosporus made him master of the whole Roman world — and cleared the road to Nicaea…
body: For a decade after the Edict of Milan (313) the uneasy partnership of Constantine and Licinius wore down to war. Beaten at Adrianople in July 324 and stripped of his fleet in the Hellespont, Licinius abandoned Byzantium and made his last stand on the Asian shore, at Chrysopolis, beneath Chalcedon.

There, on 18 September 324, Constantine broke him. Eusebius, who wrote within living memory, sets the two camps in a parable: the labarum and the ministers of God with the one, Egyptian diviners and soothsayers with the other. The defeated left some five and twenty thousand on the field by the earliest reckoning; Licinius fled to Nicomedia and there surrendered, spared at the prayer of his wife Constantia, the victor's sister — and put to death the next year on a charge of conspiracy.

Constantine stood at last sole Augustus, and the Church entered a new world. Within the year he summoned the bishops to Nicaea; within six he refounded Byzantium as his city, dedicated in 330, on the very strait where the last battle had been won.
